title: Shared State: Arc and Mutex
intro: To share one value between threads you need two things. `Arc` gives the value several owners. `Mutex` makes sure only one thread changes it at a time.

coming_from.go: A Rust `Mutex` holds the data inside it, instead of sitting next to it like `sync.Mutex`. `lock()` gives you a guard that unlocks when it goes out of scope, like a `defer mu.Unlock()` you cannot forget, and `Arc` lets several threads own the value because a Rust value has one owner, and a thread can outlive the scope that made it.
coming_from.kotlin: `Mutex` replaces `synchronized(lock)`, but the data lives inside the mutex, so you can't reach `results` without locking. `Arc` is a shared, reference-counted pointer that lets each thread own a handle to the same value.
coming_from.python: `results.lock().unwrap()` is your `with lock:`, and the lock is released when the guard goes out of scope. The data lives inside the `Mutex`, so forgetting to lock is a compile error, not a latent race that your tests may never show.
coming_from.typescript: Workers share only raw bytes in a `SharedArrayBuffer`; here `Arc<Mutex<Vec<i32>>>` shares an ordinary `Vec` between threads. `lock()` gives a guard that unlocks when it goes out of scope, and you can't touch the data without it.
coming_from.java: `Arc` gives a value several owners, the way GC references share an object between threads, and `Mutex<T>` is `synchronized` with the data inside the lock. You can only reach the `Vec` by calling `lock()`, so forgetting to lock doesn't compile.
coming_from.csharp: `Mutex<T>` is a `lock` that owns the data it protects, and `Arc<T>` shares it between threads where C# would rely on the garbage collector. The lock opens when you call `lock()` and closes at the end of the scope, and touching the data without it is a compile error.
coming_from.c: `Mutex<T>` is a `pthread_mutex_t` stored together with the data, where the data is only reachable through `lock()`. `Arc` is an atomic reference count that frees the value when the last owner drops it; an unlocked write won't compile.
coming_from.cpp: `Arc<T>` is `std::shared_ptr<T>`, and `Mutex<T>` is a `std::mutex` that wraps the data; `lock()` returns a guard like `std::lock_guard`. You can't reach the data without the guard, and sharing a type that isn't thread-safe, such as `Rc`, is a compile error.

notes: `Arc::clone` does not copy the Vec. It adds one to an atomic counter and gives you another pointer to the same Vec. When the last Arc goes away, the Vec is freed.

In many languages the mutex sits next to the data, and you have to remember to lock it. In Rust the Mutex holds the data. The only way to reach the Vec is `lock()`, so forgetting to lock does not compile.
The lock is released automatically when the value returned by `lock()` goes away, at the end of the line here. There is no `Unlock` to forget.

gotcha.title: Several threads writing to one list, without a lock
gotcha.looks_fine: The Go and Kotlin versions compile and run. Both are data races: when two threads add at the same moment, a value can be lost and the count comes out below 3. Go only reports it if you run with `-race`, which is what the Go output shows. Kotlin gives no warning.
gotcha.rust_sees: The first thread's `move` takes `results`. The second loop pass has nothing left to give. Sharing one Vec between three threads needs shared ownership and a lock, which is `Arc<Mutex<_>>` (or scoped threads that borrow a `Mutex`, shown below).
gotcha.why: Code like this really is broken in most languages, and Rust refuses to build it. Safe Rust has no data races, because it checks before the program runs: a value shared between threads must be wrapped in something that controls access. What it does not check is the logic around the locks (see the sections on deadlocks and check-then-act). Careful with the compiler's `help:` here. It suggests cloning the Vec. Once you also make the copy `mut`, that compiles, but each thread would push into its own private copy, and `results` would stay empty. Arc and Mutex are the real fix.

kotlin.says: Kotlin printed 3 this time, but this is still a race. `ArrayList` isn't safe across threads (the Java docs say so), so another run can lose items.

python.says: Python prints [0, 10, 20], because a single `append` is atomic in CPython. A read-then-write is not: the Python FAQ lists `i = i + 1` as not atomic, and the Python section below shows which counter forms lose updates.

typescript.says: Prints [], an empty list. Each worker runs the file again and pushes into its own copy of `results`, so the main thread's list never changes.

java.says: ArrayList is not thread-safe, so adds from different threads overwrite each other. The count comes out far below 400000 and changes every run.

csharp.says: Two threads add to the same List with no lock, and the count comes up short of 10000000 (it changes every run). Without the capacity set up front, the List can also throw while it grows.
